title: Finishing Halves
question: A task uses 30 minutes, then 15, then 7.5, with every later stage taking half as long. Although there are infinitely many stages in the model, their total duration approaches one hour.
correctExplanation: Correct. The geometric durations add to 30 + 15 + 7.5 + ..., whose limit is 60 minutes.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Infinitely many positive terms can have a finite sum when they shrink quickly enough; here each remaining tail is half the previous one.
lessonContent:
An infinite series describes the limit of its finite partial sums.
Geometric series converge when each term is multiplied by a fixed ratio below one in magnitude.
The number of terms and the size of their total are separate questions.
Zeno-style puzzles exploit the intuition that infinity must always produce endless duration.
Share this: add 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 on paper and watch how the gap changes.

title: Equal Time Markers
question: A machine must clear infinitely many checkpoints, and each checkpoint takes exactly one second. Unlike shrinking-time versions of Zeno's setup, this process cannot finish in a finite number of seconds.
correctExplanation: Right. Adding one second infinitely often diverges, so the elapsed time has no finite bound.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Infinity alone does not decide completion; the decisive feature is whether the required durations shrink fast enough for their sum to converge.
lessonContent:
Some infinite series converge while others diverge.
A fixed positive cost repeated without end creates an unbounded total.
To evaluate an infinite process, inspect the sizes of its stages rather than merely counting them.
This distinction separates mathematical resolutions from verbal appeals to infinity.
Share this: compare repeated one-second steps with repeatedly halved seconds.

title: The Closing Gap
question: A runner moves at 10 m/s while a tortoise 9 metres ahead moves at 1 m/s. Their relative speed is 9 m/s, so the runner catches the tortoise after one second despite any infinite subdivision of the chase.
correctExplanation: Exactly. The 9-metre lead closes at 9 metres per second, giving a finite catch time of one second.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Relative motion computes the meeting directly: initial gap divided by closing speed, independent of how many intermediate positions we name.
lessonContent:
Relative speed measures how quickly the distance between moving objects changes.
Meeting time equals initial separation divided by closing speed when speeds are constant.
Subdividing a trajectory does not change the trajectory's physical duration.
Direct models can reveal what an infinite verbal decomposition obscures.
Share this: estimate when two walkers will meet using only their gap and closing speed.

title: Endless Catch-Ups
question: Because a faster runner can be described as reaching infinitely many points previously occupied by a slower runner, the overtake must occur only after an infinite amount of time.
correctExplanation: Correct. Those successive travel times can shrink geometrically and sum to a finite meeting time.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. An infinite list of ever-shorter intervals does not imply infinite elapsed time; convergence is precisely the missing reasoning step.
lessonContent:
An infinite decomposition can fit inside a finite interval.
Each stage's duration matters more than the bare fact that stages are countable.
Convergent sums explain how a limit can be reached without a final largest subinterval.
The paradox arises by sliding from 'infinitely many descriptions' to 'endless time.'
Share this: ask a friend whether infinitely many shrinking intervals must last forever, then test a geometric example.

title: Midpoint Deadline
question: A runner travels 8 metres at a constant 8 m/s. Describing the route as 4 metres, then 2, then 1, and so on makes the journey take two seconds rather than one.
correctExplanation: Right. The segment times are 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ... seconds, which total one second.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. Partitioning the same eight-metre route into infinitely many pieces does not add distance or time; the pieces sum back to the original journey.
lessonContent:
A partition divides an existing quantity rather than duplicating it.
At constant speed, halving distance also halves the time for that segment.
The partial sums approach the original whole from below.
Changing a description cannot by itself change the motion being described.
Share this: divide a one-minute interval into halves and verify that no extra minute appears.

title: Frozen Instants
question: An arrow occupies one exact position at every instant. Therefore its position is the same at all instants, so motion is logically impossible.
correctExplanation: Correct. Having one position at each instant does not mean having one unchanged position across different instants.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. The argument confuses 'a definite position at each time' with 'the same position at every time'; a position function can vary continuously.
lessonContent:
Zeno's arrow shifts attention from intervals to durationless instants.
A function may assign one value to each input while assigning different values to different inputs.
Motion is represented by how position varies with time, not by an object being spread across positions at once.
Quantifier shifts often create the appearance of contradiction.
Share this: compare 'one seat per passenger' with 'the same seat for every passenger.'

title: Speed at Noon
question: A car can have a nonzero instantaneous speed at exactly noon even though the single instant noon has zero duration, because speed is defined by the limiting change around that instant.
correctExplanation: Exactly. Instantaneous velocity is a limit of nearby position changes divided by nearby time changes.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. The car need not travel a positive distance 'during' a durationless instant; calculus defines its velocity from behavior over shrinking surrounding intervals.
lessonContent:
Instantaneous velocity is a derivative, built from a limit of average velocities.
The interval shrinks toward zero without requiring division by zero.
Local rates can be well-defined even when an isolated instant has no duration.
Calculus answers the arrow paradox by formalizing change at a point.
Share this: inspect a speedometer and explain why its reading is not distance traveled in one instant.

title: Invented Rest Stops
question: If a route contains infinitely many mathematical points, a traveller must physically stop at every point before reaching the destination.
correctExplanation: Right. Passing through a point does not entail pausing there, so the argument inserts extra tasks into continuous motion.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. A journey can include every point on a continuous path without treating those points as separate stops requiring time.
lessonContent:
Mathematical points mark locations; they do not automatically represent actions.
Crossing, arriving, and stopping are different predicates.
A decomposition becomes misleading when it adds work absent from the original process.
Continuous motion visits positions without scheduling a pause at each one.
Share this: walk across a room and notice that named floor points do not become rest stops.

title: The Missing Metre
question: A robot moves 1/2 metre, then 1/4, then 1/8, continuing the pattern. The limiting total is one metre, so the model leaves no positive final gap.
correctExplanation: Correct. After n moves the remaining gap is 1/2^n metre, and that remainder tends to zero.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Every finite stage leaves a gap, but there is no fixed positive gap left in the limit; the remainders become smaller than any chosen distance.
lessonContent:
A limit can equal a boundary never reached by any earlier partial sum.
Remainders provide a direct way to test whether a positive gap survives.
'There is always some gap at a finite stage' does not imply 'one gap remains after all stages.'
Limits distinguish every finite approximation from the value approached.
Share this: choose a tiny tolerance and find how many halvings make the remainder smaller.

title: The Harmonic Road
question: A journey assigns 1/2 second to its first stage, 1/3 to the next, then 1/4, and so on. Because each stage shrinks toward zero, the total travel time must be finite.
correctExplanation: Correct. The harmonic tail shrinks too slowly, and 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... diverges.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. Terms approaching zero are necessary for convergence but not sufficient; their rate of decrease decides whether the total stays bounded.
lessonContent:
For a series to converge, its terms must approach zero, but that condition alone is not enough.
Slowly shrinking terms can accumulate without bound.
Comparing a new series with known benchmarks helps classify its behavior.
Infinity reasoning requires rates, not just direction of change.
Share this: contrast the first ten terms of a harmonic sum with a halving sum.

title: Counting Versus Timing
question: Two processes may each contain infinitely many modeled stages while one finishes in finite time and the other does not, because their stage durations can form different series.
correctExplanation: Right. A geometric schedule can converge while a fixed-duration or harmonic schedule diverges.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Equal stage counts do not imply equal total duration; the sequence of costs determines the sum.
lessonContent:
Cardinality counts stages but does not measure their combined duration.
Infinite sets can support totals with very different magnitudes.
Convergence is a property of the values being added, not merely how many there are.
This separation dissolves many verbal arguments that use 'infinite' as a single-size label.
Share this: invent one convergent and one divergent schedule with infinitely many stages.

title: The Final Half
question: To reach the endpoint of a halving sequence, a traveller must complete a final smallest segment immediately before arrival.
correctExplanation: Correct. The sequence has no smallest positive segment and no last term, yet its partial sums have a finite limit.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. Infinite ordered sequences need not have a final member; arrival is represented by the limit of all finite partial journeys, not by one last half.
lessonContent:
An infinite sequence can have a limit without having a final term.
Every candidate for the smallest positive half has an even smaller successor.
Expecting a last member imports finite-list structure into an infinite order.
Limit points can bound a sequence without appearing among its earlier terms.
Share this: ask what the last decimal of 0.333... would be and examine the hidden assumption.

title: The Switching Limit
question: A lamp switches on at 1/2 minute, off at 3/4, on at 7/8, and continues alternating before one minute. The instructions alone do not specify its state exactly at one minute.
correctExplanation: Correct. There is no final switch whose parity settles the state, so the finite-stage rule underdetermines the limit state.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Every time before the deadline has a later switch, and no last operation determines what must hold at the boundary.
lessonContent:
A supertask compresses infinitely many operations into a finite interval.
Rules that determine every finite stage may still fail to determine a boundary value.
Alternation need not converge just because the operation times converge.
Distinguish the limit of event times from the limit of system states.
Share this: compare an alternating sequence with a steadily shrinking numerical sequence.

title: Infinite Parity
question: In an endlessly alternating lamp supertask, the lamp must finish off because every on-switch is eventually followed by an off-switch.
correctExplanation: Right. Every off-switch is also followed by an on-switch, so that symmetric argument cannot select either final state.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. The reasoning favors one half of a perfectly symmetric alternation; without a last switch or an added boundary rule, neither state follows.
lessonContent:
Pairing arguments over infinite sequences require careful treatment of boundaries.
A claim that applies symmetrically to opposite states cannot decide between them.
Finite parity depends on a last term, which an endless alternation lacks.
Supertasks expose where familiar finite reasoning silently uses an endpoint event.
Share this: test a parity argument by swapping every odd stage with an even one.

title: One Walk, Many Cuts
question: Dividing a continuous walk into infinitely many intervals does not by itself prove the walker performed infinitely many separate stop-start actions.
correctExplanation: Exactly. A mathematical partition is a way of describing one continuous action, not evidence of repeated stopping.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. The decomposition supplies conceptual boundaries, but extra physical actions require extra premises.
lessonContent:
One event can admit many descriptions and arbitrarily fine partitions.
Description count should not be confused with action count.
Continuous processes need not restart at the boundaries chosen by an observer.
This distinction separates mathematical analysis from claims about physical mechanisms.
Share this: describe one uninterrupted gesture using several different sets of intervals.

title: Across the Instants
question: If an object is motionless within each durationless instant, it follows that its position cannot differ between any two instants.
correctExplanation: Correct. A claim about what happens within each single instant does not establish equality across distinct instants.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. The conclusion shifts from each instant considered alone to a comparison between instants, which the premise never supplies.
lessonContent:
Quantifiers can change an argument when 'each' quietly becomes 'the same across all.'
Pointwise facts do not automatically establish relationships between different points.
Motion concerns variation across time, so cross-time comparison is essential.
Many paradoxes hide their leap in a small grammatical shift.
Share this: rewrite one 'each' statement today and check whether it secretly became 'the same.'

title: Opposing Rows
question: Two carts move in opposite directions at 1 m/s each. In one second, either cart moves 1 metre relative to the ground but 2 metres relative to the other cart.
correctExplanation: Correct. Opposite velocities differ by 2 m/s, so their relative separation changes twice as fast as either ground-relative displacement.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. The measurements use different reference frames: one compares cart with ground, the other compares cart with an oppositely moving cart.
lessonContent:
Velocity is measured relative to a chosen reference frame.
Opposite motions add when calculating closing or separating speed.
Different relative displacements can describe the same event without contradiction.
Zeno's stadium puzzle pressures intuition about moving rows and time intervals.
Share this: from a moving walkway, compare your speed relative to the floor and another walker.

title: Frame Confusion
question: If a moving block passes one ground marker but two oppositely moving blocks in the same interval, the unequal counts prove that the interval had two different lengths of time.
correctExplanation: Right. The same elapsed time can produce different encounter counts because relative speeds differ.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. Counting passed objects mixes reference frames; faster relative motion explains the larger count without splitting time itself.
lessonContent:
Encounter rates depend on both spacing and relative velocity.
Counts gathered against different moving frames are not directly interchangeable.
A shared time interval can contain different numbers of crossings.
Reference-frame bookkeeping prevents apparent contradictions in motion puzzles.
Share this: count objects passed while walking with and against a crowd.

title: Smallest Step Rescue
question: Assuming space has a smallest possible length would automatically solve every Zeno paradox, including the arrow's question about velocity at an instant.
correctExplanation: Correct. A spatial cutoff may block endless distance division, but it does not by itself define time, velocity, or change at an instant.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. Solving one infinite-divisibility concern does not automatically answer the distinct conceptual problem posed by instantaneous motion.
lessonContent:
A proposed solution should be matched to the exact premise creating the puzzle.
Zeno's arguments form a family rather than one repeated argument.
Changing the structure of space leaves separate questions about time and rates.
A fix that addresses one mechanism should not be generalized without proof.
Share this: when one fix is called universal, list which assumptions it actually changes.

title: Infinity Has Types
question: From the fact that one infinite series has a finite sum, it does not follow that every infinite series has a finite sum.
correctExplanation: Right. Convergence depends on how terms behave; geometric and harmonic examples already lead to different outcomes.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. One successful convergent construction is a counterexample to 'all infinite sums diverge,' not a proof that all infinite sums converge.
lessonContent:
Existence claims and universal claims carry different logical burdens.
One convergent series proves that finite infinite sums are possible.
Classifying another series requires examining its own terms or applying a convergence test.
Infinity is not a single arithmetic behavior shared by every sequence.
Share this: whenever you learn one infinite example, ask whether it proves possibility or universality.

title: Decimal Footsteps
question: A traveller covers 0.9 metre, then 0.09, then 0.009, continuing the pattern. The infinite total equals one metre rather than stopping a tiny positive distance short.
correctExplanation: Exactly. The partial totals are 0.9, 0.99, 0.999, ..., and their limit is exactly 1.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. There is no fixed positive remainder: after n stages the gap is 10^-n metre, which can be made smaller than any positive tolerance.
lessonContent:
Repeating decimals are limits of sequences of terminating decimals.
Equality at the limit does not require a final repeated digit.
A supposed positive gap must have a definite size, which shrinking remainders eventually beat.
Decimal notation offers a familiar version of Zeno's endpoint issue.
Share this: challenge someone to name a positive gap between 0.999... and 1.

title: Boundary Without Predecessor
question: The times 1/2, 3/4, 7/8, and so on are all before one second, yet they approach one second and have no latest member before it.
correctExplanation: Correct. Each listed time has a later one in the sequence, while one second is their least upper bound.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. A sequence can approach a boundary without containing a greatest term; every candidate is followed by one closer to the limit.
lessonContent:
A bounded increasing sequence need not have a largest member.
Its supremum can exist outside the sequence itself.
Finite intuition expects a penultimate event, but dense time need not provide one.
Limit reasoning replaces 'last before' with 'arbitrarily close to.'
Share this: try to name the greatest decimal strictly below 1 and test your candidate.

title: No Last Checkpoint
question: If a sequence of checkpoints has no final checkpoint before the finish line, then reaching the finish line is mathematically impossible.
correctExplanation: Right. A finite limit can follow an endless sequence without any final pre-limit member.
incorrectExplanation: It is False. The conclusion assumes arrival needs an immediate predecessor, but continuous orders and convergent sequences need not contain one.
lessonContent:
A boundary does not always have a nearest point on its lower side.
Continuous quantities differ from discrete ladders with final rungs.
Convergence explains arrival through a limit rather than a penultimate checkpoint.
Importing predecessor logic into a dense continuum creates a false obstacle.
Share this: compare the last whole number before 10 with the last real number before 10.

title: Slowing Halves
question: A robot's stage distances halve each time, but its speed also halves so every stage still takes one second. The robot never completes all stages in finite time.
correctExplanation: Correct. Distance alone shrinks, but time equals distance divided by speed, leaving one second per stage and an unbounded total.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Halving both distance and speed cancels in the time calculation, so the durations do not form a convergent series.
lessonContent:
Travel time depends on both distance and speed.
Shrinking spatial stages do not guarantee shrinking temporal stages.
Ratios can remain constant when numerator and denominator scale together.
A motion model must specify enough variables before its infinity can be classified.
Share this: halve both a route and its speed, then calculate whether travel time changes.

title: Six Second Chase
question: A runner at 6 m/s chases another at 4 m/s with a 12-metre lead. The catch occurs after six seconds, even though the chase can be decomposed into infinitely many shrinking gap-closing stages.
correctExplanation: Exactly. The gap closes at 2 m/s, and 12 divided by 2 gives six seconds.
incorrectExplanation: It is True. Relative speed fixes the meeting time directly; infinitely many named sub-stages fit within that finite interval.
lessonContent:
Closing speed subtracts velocities when objects move in the same direction.
A finite initial gap closes in finite time whenever relative speed is positive and constant.
Infinite subdivision and direct kinematics can describe the same chase.
A good model checks paradoxical language against measurable quantities.
Share this: calculate a catch-up time from two walking speeds and a starting gap.
